title: Devlens Analysis: What the ICJ ruling can and cannot change
excerpt: The verdict due today is binding and final, but it cannot feed the camps or send anyone home. What it means for Bangladesh, donors and NGOs in Cox's Bazar.
content:
DEVLENS ANALYSIS · Humanitarian and Rohingya response · 19 November 2026

Today the International Court of Justice (ICJ) gives its judgment in The Gambia's case against Myanmar under the Genocide Convention. For the Rohingya it is the most important legal moment since the 2017 military operations that drove more than 700,000 people into Bangladesh. For the agencies and NGOs that run the response in Cox's Bazar and Bhasan Char, the harder question is what changes tomorrow. Devlens read the case documents summarised by Human Rights Watch (HRW), the statements made in Dhaka this week and the latest funding figures. Our reading: the ruling can change the politics around the Rohingya, but on its own it will not change the money, the camps or the timetable for return.

What the court is deciding

The Gambia filed the case in November 2019 with the backing of the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. It asks the court to find that Myanmar breached the convention, including by committing genocide, conspiring to commit it, failing to prevent it and failing to put suspects on trial. It is a case between states about state responsibility. No individual can be convicted in it.

According to HRW's summary of the case, The Gambia has asked for:

  • Genocide laws in Myanmar and trials of alleged perpetrators
  • Reparations, including safe return, property restitution, family reunification and protection of the Rohingya's right to identify as Rohingya
  • Compensation or other forms of satisfaction where full reparation is not possible
  • Assurances that the crimes will not be repeated, and a finding that Myanmar ignored the court's January 2020 provisional measures

Myanmar says its 2017 operations had no genocidal intent and that the evidence is weak. It has filed 12 reports on its compliance with the 2020 order, which The Gambia says give "no reason to conclude" that it complied.

Binding, final and hard to enforce

The judgment is final, with no appeal, and legally binding on both parties under Article 59 of the court's statute and Article 94(1) of the UN Charter. If Myanmar does not comply, The Gambia can go to the UN Security Council, which may recommend or decide measures under Article 94(2). HRW notes that the Security Council has never used that power. Kelley Currie, the UN Special Rapporteur on Myanmar, said in Dhaka on 18 November that China and Russia shield Myanmar at the council, The Daily Star reported.

So a finding against Myanmar would mostly work through pressure: from the UN General Assembly, from the 11 countries that joined the case as interveners (Canada, Denmark, France, Germany, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom, Maldives, Slovenia, the Democratic Republic of Congo, Belgium and Ireland), and from parallel cases. The International Criminal Court prosecutor asked for an arrest warrant for Min Aung Hlaing in November 2024, and a court in Argentina issued warrants for 25 people, including him, in February 2025.

Return is not on the table yet

Dhaka's position is clear. State Minister for Foreign Affairs Shama Obaed Islam said on 18 November that accountability is "essential to delivering justice" and that repatriation is "the only viable and durable solution", The Business Standard reported, citing UNB. But no one in a position to make return happen expects it soon. The commissioner told The Daily Star that repatriation "will not happen immediately as a direct consequence of the judgment". Thomas Kean of the International Crisis Group told Al Jazeera that the Arakan Army, which controls much of Rakhine State, "can hardly make guarantees around safety while a war is going on".

Refugees themselves want both justice and a way home. "We want to go back," Mohammad Zubair of the Arakan Rohingya Society for Peace and Human Rights told Al Jazeera. A ruling that names what happened to them, and orders reparations that include safe return and restitution, would give them and Bangladesh a stronger legal basis for those demands in any future talks. It does not create the conditions for return.

The money problem the verdict does not solve

The response is running on less. The 2026 Joint Response Plan seeks $710.5 million for 1.56 million refugees and host community members, 26% less than the 2025 appeal, UNHCR told The Daily Star. Since April, the World Food Programme has paid most refugees less than the old flat $12 a person a month, and the Refugee Relief and Repatriation Commissioner, Mohammed Mizanur Rahman, said this tiered system is funded only until April 2027. WFP had warned in September that general food assistance could be interrupted from December 2026 without more money, the paper reported. Among children aged 6 to 59 months, acute malnutrition reached 14.6% in the 2026 Nutrition SMART Survey. UNHCR figures cited by the paper put it at 8.6% in 2024 and 13.9% in 2025.

Education is in a similar state. HRW said on 16 November that donor-funded programmes enrol 312,000 of about 500,000 school-age children, and that donors had pledged $36 million of a $53 million request for 2026 by mid-October. Currie said cuts to protection, education and livelihoods are pushing people towards drugs, trafficking and armed group recruitment, and that gender-based violence and serious crimes against children are rising.

A judgment cannot pay for rations. But it may move donor attention, and the timing matters: governments are setting their 2027 humanitarian budgets now. A finding of genocide would make it harder for donors to argue that the Rohingya are a lower priority, while a narrower ruling could let attention drift further.

What this means for NGOs

  • Expect questions in the camps. Refugees plan to watch the verdict together, and many will hope it means early return. Community engagement and protection teams should be ready to explain plainly what the court can and cannot do.
  • Watch for tension and risk. Currie warned of the risk of renewed violence in Myanmar. A strong verdict could raise expectations; a weak one could deepen frustration. Both can affect safety in the camps and new arrivals at the border.
  • Use the moment for funding advocacy. The case for 2027 pledges for food, nutrition, education and protection is easier to make while the world is watching. National NGOs, which deliver much of the frontline work, have a strong claim to direct funding.
  • Keep host communities in view. Cox's Bazar residents carry much of the cost of the response, and their support will matter in whatever comes next.

What to watch

The wording of the judgment, especially on genocidal intent and reparations; Myanmar's response; whether The Gambia or others take the ruling to the Security Council; statements by donors at the end of the year; and whether the verdict shows up in 2027 funding for the Joint Response Plan. Devlens will report the ruling once it is delivered.
